name: Persian Gulf → China
sellers: Saudi Arabia, the largest crude exporter through Hormuz.
buyers: China, one of the four Asian buyers taking most Hormuz crude.
why_it_matters: Most crude leaving Hormuz goes to Asia, and this corridor crosses both Hormuz and Malacca.
situation: Halted: Hormuz has been largely blocked since the end of February 2026, with transits down to a handful a day.

name: Persian Gulf → India
sellers: Iraq, the second-largest crude exporter through Hormuz.
buyers: India, which together with China took a large share of the crude leaving the strait.
why_it_matters: Iraq was a leading supplier to Indian refiners and has no export outlet that avoids Hormuz.
situation: Iraqi cargoes to India all but vanished after Hormuz closed; Indian refiners turned to Saudi crude from Yanbu, UAE crude from Fujairah and more Russian barrels.

name: Persian Gulf → Japan
sellers: Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which together supply most of Japan’s crude.
buyers: Japan, among the importers most reliant on crude passing through Hormuz.
why_it_matters: Most of Japan’s crude arrives on this corridor through Hormuz and Malacca.
situation: Blocked at Hormuz. Japan is importing a fraction of its usual volumes, drawing on reserves and on Middle Eastern crude loaded outside the strait at Yanbu and Fujairah.

name: Persian Gulf → South Korea
sellers: Saudi Arabia above all, then the UAE.
buyers: South Korea, one of the four top destinations of Hormuz crude.
why_it_matters: Most Korean crude imports transited Hormuz, which makes Korean refiners highly exposed to the strait.
situation: Blocked at Hormuz. South Korea has become one of the largest buyers of Saudi crude rerouted through Yanbu on the Red Sea.

name: Persian Gulf → Europe (Suez route)
sellers: Saudi Arabia and other Gulf exporters.
buyers: European refiners, which take only a small share of Gulf crude.
why_it_matters: This was the default Gulf-to-Europe route until Red Sea attacks pushed tankers away from it.
situation: Halted upstream by the Hormuz closure.

name: Persian Gulf → Europe (via the Cape)
sellers: Saudi Arabia and other Gulf exporters.
buyers: European refiners.
why_it_matters: The Cape detour keeps Gulf crude reaching Europe without the Red Sea, at the cost of a much longer voyage.
situation: Halted upstream: cargoes load inside the Gulf, behind the closed Strait of Hormuz.

name: Yanbu (Red Sea) → Europe — Hormuz bypass
sellers: Saudi Arabia, shipping from its Red Sea coast.
buyers: European refiners, supplied through the Suez Canal and the SUMED pipeline.
why_it_matters: The Red Sea outlet lets Saudi crude avoid Hormuz, and Saudi Arabia already leaned on it during the Red Sea attacks.
situation: The main Hormuz bypass during the war. Once the Houthi blockade threatened Yanbu-to-Asia voyages, Saudi crude was increasingly pumped through SUMED to Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, mostly for Europe and the US — until the East-West pipeline was shut after drone attacks in September 2026.

name: Fujairah → India — Hormuz bypass
sellers: The UAE, loading outside the strait.
buyers: Indian refiners.
why_it_matters: Fujairah lets UAE crude avoid Hormuz, but before the war it carried only a secondary share of UAE crude to India.
situation: Since Hormuz closed, almost all UAE crude bound for India loads at Fujairah.

name: Russia (Baltic) → India
buyers: India, the main destination of Russia’s western crude since the war in Ukraine.
why_it_matters: Russian crude became a major feedstock for Indian refiners, on a long voyage through the Danish Straits and Suez.
situation: Indian imports of Russian crude rose again after Hormuz closed.

name: Russia (Pacific) → China
sellers: Russia, shipping ESPO crude from its Pacific coast.
buyers: Chinese refiners.
why_it_matters: A short haul with no chokepoint, and a growing share of Chinese seaborne crude imports.

name: Russia (Black Sea) → India
sellers: Russia and Caspian producers loading in the Black Sea, with Kazakhstan the largest exporter through the Turkish Straits.
buyers: India.
why_it_matters: Part of the western Russian crude swung from Europe to India, crossing both the Turkish Straits and Suez.
situation: Indian imports of Russian crude rose again after Hormuz closed.

name: United States (Gulf of Mexico) → Europe
sellers: The United States, from its Gulf Coast.
buyers: European refiners, the top destination for US crude since 2023.
why_it_matters: US crude gained ground in Europe after the war in Ukraine, on an Atlantic crossing with no chokepoint.

name: Angola → China
buyers: China, by far Angola’s largest crude buyer.
why_it_matters: West African crude is one of the big flows rounding the Cape eastbound to Asia.

name: Brazil (pre-salt) → China
buyers: China, the leading buyer of Brazilian crude.
why_it_matters: South American crude is among the largest flows going around the Cape to Asia.

name: Persian Gulf → Europe (diesel & jet fuel)
buyers: Europe, which turned to Middle Eastern and US diesel after banning Russian products.
why_it_matters: Gulf diesel filled part of the gap left by Russian barrels, though most Gulf products still go to Asia.
situation: Halted by the Hormuz closure.

name: India → Europe (via the Cape)
sellers: India, led by the Jamnagar refining complex.
buyers: European diesel importers.
why_it_matters: Indian diesel sails to Europe around the Cape, where product traffic jumped after the Red Sea attacks.
situation: Indian diesel loadings for Europe recovered in July 2026 to pre-war levels.

name: United States → Brazil (diesel & gasoline)
buyers: Brazil.
why_it_matters: US distillate exports to Brazil more than doubled in a year.

name: US Gulf → Europe (diesel)
buyers: Europe, with the Netherlands and the United Kingdom as main outlets.
why_it_matters: US diesel is one of Europe’s replacements for Russian products since the EU ban.

name: Russia (Baltic) → Turkey & the Mediterranean
buyers: Turkey, which buys most of its diesel from Russia.
why_it_matters: Turkey depends on Russian diesel, and Baltic cargoes now head to Türkiye rather than north-west Europe.
situation: Deliveries fell in mid-2026 after Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and Moscow halted diesel exports in July.

name: Persian Gulf → East Africa
sellers: Saudi Arabia and the UAE, through their state oil companies.
buyers: Kenya.
why_it_matters: Kenya imports its fuel under a government-to-government deal with Gulf suppliers.
situation: The Hormuz closure trapped a cargo in Dubai and pushed Kenyan importers to buy expensive loads outside the deal.

name: United States → South American Pacific coast (via Panama)
buyers: Chile and other Pacific-coast importers.
why_it_matters: Chile is the second-largest outlet for US distillate, and refined products dominate oil traffic through Panama.

name: Qatar → China
buyers: China, the largest buyer of Qatari LNG.
why_it_matters: Asia takes most Qatari LNG, and Qatar-to-China cargoes are a growing share of the gas crossing Malacca.
situation: Halted: with no alternative route, the closure has cut off about a fifth of global LNG supply, most of it Qatari.

name: Qatar → Europe (via the Cape)
buyers: European importers, with Italy the most dependent on Qatari LNG.
why_it_matters: Europe takes only a small share of the LNG leaving Hormuz, but some countries rely heavily on it.
situation: Europe’s imports of Qatari LNG fell from March 2026 as the closure limited Qatari exports.

name: United States → Europe
sellers: The United States, the world’s largest LNG exporter.
buyers: Europe, which received most US cargoes.
why_it_matters: Most US cargoes go to Europe, where LNG imports grew faster than in any other region.

name: United States → Japan (via Panama)
buyers: Japan and other Asian importers.
why_it_matters: Panama gives US LNG a much shorter route to Japan than the Cape or Suez.

name: Australia (North West Shelf) → Japan
sellers: Australia, one of the three largest LNG exporters.
buyers: Japan, one of Australia’s two largest LNG markets.
why_it_matters: A major LNG trade on a route with no Middle East exposure.
situation: Japan was again Australia’s largest LNG market in the first half of 2026.

name: Australia (Queensland) → China
buyers: China, the largest LNG importer and Australia’s largest LNG customer in 2024.
why_it_matters: Chinese demand shapes Australian LNG exports, and it softened as China’s LNG imports fell.

name: Russia (Yamal) → Europe
sellers: Russia, from the Yamal LNG plant.
buyers: EU importers, which take most Yamal cargoes.
why_it_matters: Yamal is a sizeable share of EU LNG imports, with an EU ban on Russian LNG approaching.
situation: EU imports from Yamal reached a record in the first half of 2026.

name: Russia (Yamal) → China via the Northern Sea Route
sellers: Russia, from the Yamal LNG plant.
buyers: China.
why_it_matters: The Northern Sea Route opens a summer outlet to Asia for Arctic LNG.
situation: Asia-bound Yamal volumes collapsed in the first half of 2026 as Europe absorbed the plant’s output.

name: Indonesia → China
sellers: Indonesia, the world’s top coal exporter.
buyers: China, the world’s largest coal importer.
why_it_matters: Indonesian coal flows to China swing with Chinese stocks and demand.

name: Indonesia → India
buyers: India, where Indonesia remains the main supplier.
why_it_matters: India’s power sector depends on seaborne coal, and Indonesian shipments are losing share to South Africa and Russia.

name: Australia → Japan
buyers: Japan, historically the largest market for Australian coal.
why_it_matters: Japan remains a core buyer of Australian coal even as its share shrinks.

name: Australia → China (metallurgical coal)
sellers: Australia, from its Queensland coking coal ports.
buyers: Chinese steelmakers.
why_it_matters: Australian coking coal feeds Chinese steel mills, in a market sensitive to China’s import appetite.
situation: Australian coking coal shipments to China jumped in June 2026.

name: Australia → South Korea
buyers: South Korea, where Australia is the largest coal supplier.
why_it_matters: Australia is Korea’s largest coal supplier while Korean imports decline.

name: South Africa → India
buyers: India, the main outlet for South African coal.
why_it_matters: South African coal is gaining share in India at Indonesia’s expense.

name: Russia (Far East) → China
sellers: Russia, from its Far East ports.
buyers: China.
why_it_matters: Russia sends most of its coal to Asia, and China is a key outlet partly served by rail.

name: Australia (Pilbara) → China
sellers: Australia, the largest seaborne iron ore exporter.
buyers: China, which absorbs most seaborne iron ore.
why_it_matters: The workhorse of global dry bulk, on a short haul to North Asia.

name: Brazil → China
sellers: Brazil, the second-largest seaborne iron ore exporter.
buyers: China, the main buyer of Brazilian ore.
why_it_matters: A long-haul trade that keeps large ore carriers employed for weeks per voyage.

name: Brazil → Europe
buyers: European steelmakers, a modest share of seaborne ore demand.
why_it_matters: Europe is a small but steady outlet for Brazilian ore beside China.

name: Australia → Japan & Korea
buyers: Japan and South Korea, the next largest ore importers after China.
why_it_matters: North Asian steelmakers outside China rely on the same Pilbara ore flows.

name: Guinea (Simandou) → China
sellers: Guinea, from the new Simandou project.
buyers: China.
why_it_matters: Simandou adds a large new source of iron ore for China outside Australia and Brazil.

name: Brazil → China (soybeans)
buyers: China, which takes most Brazilian soybeans.
why_it_matters: China takes most of Brazil’s record soybean exports, and Brazil has also overtaken the US as China’s corn supplier.

name: United States (Mississippi) → China (via Panama)
sellers: US farmers and exporters shipping from the Mississippi Gulf.
buyers: China, historically the largest buyer of US soybeans.
why_it_matters: US–China trade policy decides this flow: purchases collapsed in 2025 before a trade deal.

name: United States (Pacific Northwest) → Japan
sellers: US wheat growers shipping from the Pacific Northwest.
buyers: Japanese flour millers.
why_it_matters: Japan is a steady buyer of US wheat.

name: Ukraine → Egypt & North Africa
sellers: Ukraine, shipping through the Odesa ports.
buyers: Egypt, a major wheat importer.
why_it_matters: Ukrainian wheat has been winning share in Egypt as Russia’s dominance there weakens.

name: Russia → Egypt & the Middle East (wheat)
sellers: Russia, a leading grain exporter shipping mostly wheat.
buyers: Egypt, the second buyer of Russian grain after Turkey.
why_it_matters: Egypt buys Russian grain almost entirely as wheat.

name: Argentina → China (soy)
sellers: Argentina, which mostly exports soybean meal and oil.
buyers: China.
why_it_matters: Argentine soy sales to China ran well above average in 2025.

name: Australia → China (barley)
buyers: China, which takes most Australian barley.
why_it_matters: Barley is one of Australia’s most China-dependent grain exports.

name: Guinea → China (bauxite)
buyers: Chinese alumina refiners.
why_it_matters: Guinea supplies most of China’s bauxite, and a record share of its shipments went to China.

name: Chile → China (copper concentrate)
buyers: Chinese copper smelters.
why_it_matters: Chile is China’s largest source of copper concentrate.

name: Peru → China (copper concentrate)
buyers: Chinese copper smelters.
why_it_matters: Peru is China’s second source of copper concentrate.

name: Qatar → Brazil (urea)
sellers: Qatar, one of the Gulf urea exporters.
buyers: Brazilian farmers, who rely on imports for almost all their fertilizer.
why_it_matters: Brazil’s crops depend on imported nitrogen, and a large share of traded urea comes from the Gulf.
situation: Blocked at Hormuz, like the other Gulf urea exporters.

name: Persian Gulf → India (urea)
buyers: India, which bought most of its urea imports from Gulf countries.
why_it_matters: Indian agriculture depends on Gulf urea, much of it from producers inside Hormuz.
situation: Blocked at Hormuz, like the other Gulf urea exporters.

name: Morocco → Brazil (phosphates)
sellers: Morocco, holder of by far the largest phosphate rock reserves.
buyers: Brazil, whose phosphate imports come mainly from Morocco and Russia.
why_it_matters: Moroccan phosphate is a mainstay of Brazilian crop nutrition.

name: Russia (Baltic) → Brazil (potash & NPK)
buyers: Brazil, which relies on Russia and Belarus for part of its potash.
why_it_matters: Russian potash remains a key input for Brazilian agriculture.

name: DR Congo → China (copper cathodes)
buyers: China, where the DRC is now the leading source of refined copper.
why_it_matters: Congolese cathodes have become China’s main imported refined copper.

name: Chile → Japan (copper concentrate)
buyers: Japanese copper smelters, for which Chile is the largest supplier.
why_it_matters: Japan’s smelting industry depends on Chilean concentrate.

name: Australia (Weipa) → China (bauxite)
buyers: Chinese alumina refiners.
why_it_matters: Australia is China’s second bauxite supplier, far behind Guinea.

name: Australia (Gladstone) → China (alumina)
sellers: Australia, which refines most of its bauxite into alumina at home.
buyers: Chinese aluminium smelters.
why_it_matters: Australia supplied nearly all of China’s alumina imports in mid-2026.
situation: Australia supplied nearly all of China’s surging alumina imports in mid-2026.

name: United Arab Emirates → Japan (primary aluminium)
sellers: The UAE, the largest Middle Eastern source of Japan’s aluminium.
buyers: Japanese metal importers.
why_it_matters: Middle Eastern smelters supply a large share of Japan’s aluminium imports.
situation: Loading inside the Gulf, this metal is trapped by the Hormuz closure; Japanese premiums reached their highest in more than a decade.

name: Russia (Pacific) → Japan (primary aluminium)
buyers: Japanese metal importers, which bought little Russian aluminium.
why_it_matters: Japan bought far less aluminium from Russia than from the Middle East.
situation: A corridor opened by the war: Rusal plans to divert metal from China to Japan to capture record premiums.

name: Indonesia → China (nickel pig iron & ferronickel)
buyers: China.
why_it_matters: Nearly all of Indonesia’s processed nickel goes to China.

name: Philippines → China (nickel ore)
buyers: Chinese nickel processors.
why_it_matters: Most Philippine nickel ore feeds Chinese plants, and Manila dropped its planned ban on raw ore exports.

name: Philippines → Indonesia (nickel ore)
buyers: Indonesian nickel smelters.
why_it_matters: Indonesia now imports ore to feed smelting capacity that outgrew its own supply.

name: Australia → China (zinc concentrate)
sellers: Australia, holder of the largest zinc reserves.
buyers: Chinese zinc smelters.
why_it_matters: Australia is the leading supplier of zinc concentrate to China, in a tight concentrate market.

name: Peru → China (zinc & lead concentrates)
buyers: Chinese zinc smelters.
why_it_matters: Peru is China’s second zinc concentrate supplier.

name: Indonesia → China (tin)
sellers: Indonesia, the largest refined tin exporter.
buyers: China, the second destination of Indonesian tin.
why_it_matters: China is one of the two main outlets for the world’s largest refined tin exporter.

name: Guyana → Europe
sellers: Guyana, producing from the Stabroek block.
buyers: European refiners, which take most Guyanese exports.
why_it_matters: Guyana’s young offshore production mostly sails to Europe.

name: Canada → Brazil (potash)
buyers: Brazil, the second market for Canadian potash after the United States.
why_it_matters: Brazil buys Canadian potash alongside Russian and Belarusian supply.

name: Canada → China (potash)
buyers: China, a smaller outlet for Canadian potash.
why_it_matters: Canada ships potash across the North Pacific to China alongside its main markets.

name: Canada → China & Japan (wheat and canola)
sellers: Western Canadian wheat and canola growers.
buyers: China and other Asian buyers.
why_it_matters: Record grain volumes pass through Vancouver, exposed to Chinese tariff decisions on canola.

name: Colombia → Europe
buyers: Europe, which takes about half the coal from Colombia’s main terminal.
why_it_matters: Colombia’s coal exports are shrinking fast as its main outlet declines.

name: Australia → China (spodumene)
sellers: Australia, shipping spodumene from Western Australia.
buyers: China, which takes almost all Australian spodumene.
why_it_matters: The first link of the battery supply chain, though China is diversifying towards Africa.

name: Australia → Indonesia (spodumene)
buyers: Indonesia.
why_it_matters: A small but fast-growing outlet for Australian spodumene.

name: DR Congo → China (cobalt hydroxide)
buyers: Chinese cobalt refiners.
why_it_matters: Congolese export policy directly sets the supply of cobalt feed to China.

name: South Africa → China (chrome ore)
buyers: China.
why_it_matters: China takes about half of South Africa’s chrome ore, even as Pretoria moves to restrict exports.

name: South Africa → China (manganese)
sellers: South Africa, the largest manganese ore exporter.
buyers: China, which consumes most seaborne manganese ore.
why_it_matters: South Africa is China’s largest source of manganese ore.

name: Gabon → China (manganese)
buyers: China.
why_it_matters: Gabon is a major supplier to China but plans to ban raw ore exports.

name: Australia → China (manganese)
buyers: China.
why_it_matters: Australia is one of China’s leading manganese ore suppliers.

name: China → Japan (rare earth magnets)
sellers: China, which dominates rare earth refining.
buyers: Japan.
why_it_matters: China uses export controls on heavy rare earths as leverage, and Japan is directly exposed.
situation: Shipments of key heavy rare earths to Japan have stayed at zero, most recently in June 2026.

name: Malaysia → China (rare earths)
sellers: Malaysia, home to the most significant separation plant outside China.
buyers: China.
why_it_matters: Malaysia is China’s second source of rare earth imports.

name: Australia → Malaysia (rare earth concentrate)
sellers: Australia, from the Mount Weld mine.
buyers: The Kuantan separation plant in Malaysia.
why_it_matters: The main rare earth processing chain outside China runs on this flow.

name: Indonesia → Singapore (tin)
buyers: Singapore, the largest destination of Indonesian tin.
why_it_matters: Singapore acts as the main trading outlet for Indonesian refined tin.
